kurz: How the IRS taxes rental income, why depreciation and the passive activity rules decide whether a tax loss helps you, and how recapture and a 1031 exchange shape the exit.

bloecke.md:
For federal tax purposes, net rental income is ordinary income. There is no special rate for rents and no withholding by a bank or property manager. You report each property on Schedule E (Form 1040), Part I; the net result is added to your other income and taxed at your marginal rate. For 2026, the federal brackets run from 10% to 37%; the 37% rate applies to taxable income above $640,600 for single filers and $768,700 for married couples filing jointly. Most states tax rental income as well, usually at their regular income tax rates.

The result is rental income minus deductible expenses. Most individual landlords use the cash method: rent counts in the year you receive it, an expense in the year you pay it. Advance rent is income when received, whatever period it covers. A security deposit is not income as long as you plan to return it. If you keep it because the tenant did not live up to the lease, it becomes income in that year.

bloecke.titel: Tax calculation for a rented house in its second year
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation: purchase price $385,000 plus $15,000 of closing costs added to basis, 25% of it allocated to land, a 30-year fixed loan of $300,000 at 6.5%, rent of $2,600 a month, self-managed, no vacancy.

bloecke.md:
## Tax loss and cash result

The loss of $6,886 exists only on Schedule E. Two items behave differently there than in your bank account. Depreciation of $10,909 reduces taxable income although no money leaves the account. The principal portion of the mortgage payment costs money but is not deductible, because it turns cash into equity and is not an expense. Anyone who mixes up the two misreads the property: it can show a tax loss while the account balance grows, or a taxable profit while the account runs dry.

bloecke.titel: Tax return and bank statement compared
zeilen: yes, spread over the loan term
Closing costs such as title insurance, recording fees and transfer taxes
no, added to basis and recovered through depreciation (building share only)

bloecke.md:
The monthly payment on $300,000 at 6.5% over 30 years is $1,896.20, or $22,754 a year. In the second year, about $19,177 of it is interest and $3,578 principal.

- Rent +$31,200
- Mortgage payments −$22,754
- Property tax, insurance and repairs −$8,000
- Cash result +$446

Whether the tax loss of $6,886 is worth anything depends on the passive activity rules described below. A single filer in the 22% bracket with a modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of up to $100,000 can deduct it and saves about $1,515 in federal tax, so the year ends with about $1,961 in the pocket while the loan balance falls by $3,578. With a MAGI of $150,000 or more, the loss is suspended. This year, only the $446 remains, and the loss waits for later years or for the sale.

## Depreciation of the building

Depreciation is the only deductible item that costs no money. It exists only for property used to produce income; your own home cannot be depreciated. Only the building is depreciated, never the land, because land does not wear out. Residential rental property, a building in which at least 80% of the gross rents come from dwelling units, is depreciated straight-line over 27.5 years under the General Depreciation System (MACRS, 26 U.S.C. § 168). Depreciation starts when the unit is placed in service, that is, ready and available for rent, not when the first tenant moves in. A mid-month convention applies: in the month the property is placed in service and in the month it is sold, only half a month counts.

Depreciation is not optional. When you sell, your basis is reduced by the depreciation allowed or allowable, that is, by what you could have claimed, even if you never did. Skipping it saves no tax later; it only loses the deduction. Depreciation that was not claimed in earlier years can usually be caught up with Form 3115 (change in accounting method).

bloecke.formel: Depreciable basis = (Purchase price + Capitalized closing costs) × Building share
bloecke.erklaerung: The building share is usually derived from the county assessor's split between land and improvements or from an appraisal. It is not freely negotiable; the IRS accepts a reasonable, documented method.
variablen: title insurance, recording fees, transfer taxes, legal fees, surveys; loan costs and prepaid items such as escrow deposits are not included
often taken from the assessor's ratio of improvement value to total assessed value; in expensive locations, the land share is much higher
bloecke.beispiel: $400,000 × 75% = $300,000 depreciable basis; divided by 27.5 years, that is $10,909 of depreciation in a full year.

bloecke.titel: Straight-line depreciation and cost segregation on a $300,000 building over ten years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation, placed in service in January. In the second series, a cost segregation study reclassifies $60,000 as 5- and 15-year property, written off in year 1 through 100% bonus depreciation (property acquired after January 19, 2025). After ten years, $146,909 instead of $108,636 has been deducted. The total over the life of the property stays the same, and the accelerated part is taxed as ordinary income on a sale.

bloecke.md:
With a total basis of $400,000, each percentage point of building share is worth $4,000 of basis and $145 of depreciation a year. Ten percentage points therefore decide over $40,000 of deductions over 27.5 years, or $1,455 a year.

The county assessor's split is the usual starting point, but assessors value land by their own methods, and the ratio can be far off in either direction. A different allocation is possible if it is supported, for example by an appraisal that values land and building separately. An allocation in the purchase contract without an economic basis does not hold up in an audit.

## Repairs or improvements

Repairs that keep the property in its ordinary operating condition are deductible in the year you pay them: fixing a leak, repainting, replacing a broken window pane, servicing the furnace. Improvements must be capitalized and depreciated. Under the tangible property regulations, an expense is an improvement if it is a betterment, a restoration or an adaptation. A betterment makes the property better than it was, for example an addition or a higher-grade kitchen; fixing a defect that already existed when you bought the property also counts as a betterment. A restoration replaces a major component or a substantial structural part, such as the entire roof or the entire heating and cooling system. An adaptation converts the property to a new or different use. A new roof for $22,000 is therefore not a $22,000 deduction but $800 a year for 27.5 years.

Two elections let small landlords deduct immediately what would otherwise have to be capitalized. The de minimis safe harbor allows items or invoices of up to $2,500 each to be expensed. The safe harbor for small taxpayers covers all repairs, maintenance and improvements on a building with an unadjusted basis of up to $1,000,000, as long as their total for the year does not exceed the lesser of $10,000 or 2% of that basis (and average annual gross receipts do not exceed $10 million).

For the $300,000 building, the limit is $6,000. If the year's total is $6,500, the safe harbor is lost for the entire amount and not just the excess, and every item has to be checked against the improvement rules again. Anyone close to the limit can move work into the next tax year. Both elections are made each year with a statement attached to the return filed on time.

A deduction is worth as much as the marginal rate of the year in which it can actually be used. A $20,000 repair saves $2,400 in a year in the 12% bracket and $4,800 in a year in the 24% bracket. Under the cash method, the date of payment decides, so paying in December or in January shifts the deduction by a whole year. If losses are suspended anyway under the passive activity rules, timing matters less: the deduction then waits for a year with passive income or for the sale.

## Loss offsetting: the passive activity rules

Under 26 U.S.C. § 469, rental activities are passive by definition, regardless of how much work you put in. Passive losses may only offset passive income, not wages, interest, dividends or capital gains. Losses that cannot be used are suspended and carried forward indefinitely. They become fully deductible in the year you sell the property to an unrelated party in a taxable transaction.

There are two important exceptions. Under the special allowance, owners who actively participate can deduct up to $25,000 of rental losses a year against other income. Active participation requires owning at least 10% and making management decisions such as approving tenants, setting rents and approving repairs; this is possible even with a property manager. The allowance shrinks by 50 cents for every dollar of MAGI above $100,000 and is gone at $150,000. These thresholds are not indexed for inflation and have been unchanged since 1986. The second exception is real estate professional status: more than half of your working hours and more than 750 hours a year in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participate. Rental losses can then be non-passive. A full-time employee in another field practically cannot qualify.

bloecke.erklaerung: Applies to owners who actively participate; the result cannot be less than zero or more than $25,000. The calculation is made on Form 8582.
variablen: modified adjusted gross income, computed for this purpose without passive losses and certain other deductions
per return; generally $12,500 for married individuals filing separately who lived apart all year
bloecke.beispiel: MAGI $130,000: $25,000 − 50% × $30,000 = $10,000. The $6,886 loss from the example is fully deductible. At $140,000, only $5,000 would be, and $1,886 would be carried forward.

bloecke.md:
## Renting to relatives and vacation homes

If you rent a home to a relative for less than fair rental value, every day counts as personal use under 26 U.S.C. § 280A. Renting at fair rental value to a relative who uses the home as a main home does not count as personal use. For a property you also use yourself, the 14-day rule applies. If personal use exceeds the greater of 14 days or 10% of the days rented at fair rent, the property counts as a residence; expenses must be divided between rental and personal days, and rental expenses are deductible only up to the rental income, so no loss can arise. Conversely, if you rent out a home for fewer than 15 days in a year, the rent is tax-free and no rental expenses are deductible.

If there is no profit motive at all, 26 U.S.C. § 183 applies. Since 2018, the expenses of such an activity are effectively no longer deductible, while the income remains taxable.

## No tax-free holding period

The US has no holding period after which the gain on a rental property becomes tax-free. After more than one year, the gain is long-term and taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on income. The part of the gain that results from straight-line depreciation on the building, called unrecaptured section 1250 gain, is taxed at the ordinary rate but at most 25% (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)). Depreciation on 5- and 15-year property from a cost segregation study is recaptured in full as ordinary income (§ 1245). On top of this, the 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) applies to rental income and gains once MAGI exceeds $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly; these thresholds are not indexed either. A sale after one year or less is a short-term gain, taxed entirely at ordinary rates. The sale is reported on Form 4797.

bloecke.titel: How the gain on selling a home or rental is taxed
bloecke.unter: Main home means owned and used as your principal residence for at least two of the five years before the sale (26 U.S.C. § 121). Depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 is never covered by the exclusion.

felder.text: The two-year test cannot be met. A partial exclusion is possible only after a move for work, health or unforeseen circumstances; otherwise short-term gain at ordinary rates.
Exclusion for single filers or married couples filing jointly. Gain from depreciation and from rental use after 2008 before moving in remains taxable.
Short-term gain; the depreciation claimed increases it. Deferral possible only through a 1031 exchange.
0, 15 or 20% on the gain, up to 25% on the depreciation, possibly 3.8% NIIT. A 1031 exchange defers everything; a step-up at death erases it.

bloecke.titel: Depreciation and the gain on sale
bloecke.md:
A married couple buys a rental house in January 2019 for $300,000 including capitalized closing costs; $225,000 is allocated to the building. Depreciation from 2019 until the sale in January 2026 totals $57,273. They sell for $420,000 and pay $25,200 in commissions and closing costs.

Adjusted basis = 300,000 − 57,273 = $242,727

Gain = 420,000 − 25,200 − 242,727 = $152,073

Of this, $57,273 is unrecaptured section 1250 gain. With other taxable income in the 32% bracket, it is taxed at 25%, that is $14,318. The remaining $94,800 is taxed at 15%, that is $14,220, assuming it stays within the 15% capital gains bracket. If their MAGI is high enough for the full gain to fall under the NIIT, another $5,779 is added. The federal tax comes to about $34,317, before any state income tax. Passive losses suspended over the years become deductible in the year of sale and reduce the bill.

## Deferring the gain: the 1031 exchange

Under 26 U.S.C. § 1031, no gain is recognized if real property held for investment or for use in a business is exchanged for other real property of like kind. In practice, almost any US investment property counts as like kind to any other; foreign real property does not count as like kind to US property. Since 2018, only real property qualifies. The rules are strict. The sale proceeds must go to a qualified intermediary and must never be available to you. The replacement property must be identified in writing within 45 days and acquired within 180 days of the sale, but no later than the due date of the tax return including extensions. Cash or debt relief that is not reinvested (boot) is taxable. The old basis, and with it the deferred gain and the depreciation, carries over to the new property; Form 8824 documents the exchange.

The deferral can be repeated. If the owner dies while holding the property, the heirs receive a basis equal to the fair market value at death (26 U.S.C. § 1014). The deferred gain and the depreciation recapture then disappear for good. Exchanging until death is therefore a common and legal planning strategy.

Property held primarily for sale to customers is inventory, not an investment. Anyone who regularly buys, renovates and resells houses (flipping) may be treated as a dealer. The gain is then ordinary income that can also be subject to self-employment tax, the property cannot be depreciated, and a 1031 exchange is not available. There is no fixed number of transactions that triggers dealer status. Courts weigh the purpose of the purchase, the frequency of sales, the improvements and the marketing efforts. One taxpayer can hold some properties as investments and others as inventory.

## Switching between your home and a rental

If you convert your home into a rental, deductions start when the property is available for rent. The depreciable basis is the lower of your adjusted basis and the fair market value on the date of conversion; a loss in value before the conversion is never deductible. If you sell later, the § 121 exclusion is still available as long as you lived in the home for two of the last five years, so it expires three years after you move out. Depreciation claimed in the meantime is taxed in any case.

The reverse direction is less favorable. If you move into a former rental, periods of rental use after 2008 count as nonqualified use, and the corresponding share of the gain is not excluded. A property acquired in a 1031 exchange must also be owned for five years before the § 121 exclusion can apply to it.

## Landlord-tenant law as a limit on returns

In most of the United States, the market sets the rent. At the end of a lease, the landlord can offer a renewal at a new rent or, with proper notice, end a month-to-month tenancy. Rent regulation is a matter of state and local law, and many states prohibit their cities from adopting rent control. Where it exists, it can limit the return considerably.

bloecke.md:
A unit covered by the statewide cap is rented for $2,400 a month. The relevant regional consumer price index rose by 2.8%.

- Cap: 5% + 2.8% = 7.8%
- Highest new rent: $2,400 × 1.078 = $2,587.20

If inflation had been 6%, the formula would give 11%, and the 10% ceiling would apply: at most $2,640. Within twelve months, the rent may be increased at most twice, and both increases together must stay within the cap. For a buyer, the current rent and the cap therefore matter more than the market rent advertised next door.

Your tax depends on the difference between rent and deductible expenses. In the example, [[Depreciation|depreciation]] is the largest deductible item after interest and costs no money, while the principal portion of the mortgage payment costs money and is not deductible. Whether the resulting tax loss is worth anything depends on the passive activity rules, and every dollar of depreciation comes back as a taxable gain on a sale unless a 1031 exchange or a step-up at death intervenes.

bloecke.titel: Evictions, tenants' rights and buying with a tenant
bloecke.md:
Eviction requires a court order in every state. A landlord may not change the locks, remove the tenant's belongings or cut off utilities to force a tenant out. Grounds and notice periods are a matter of state law: for unpaid rent, a short notice to pay or quit is typical; ending a month-to-month tenancy usually requires 30 or 60 days' notice. Several states and cities, among them California, Oregon, New Jersey and New York City for stabilized apartments, require just cause to end a tenancy. Moving in yourself is a recognized ground in many of them, sometimes only with a relocation payment.

The federal Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability; many states add further categories, such as source of income. When you buy a rented property, existing leases generally remain in effect, and you take over the tenant and the security deposit. Under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, a tenant with a bona fide lease can generally stay until the end of the lease even after a foreclosure, with at least 90 days' notice. Buyers who want to move into a rented home must therefore plan around the lease term and the local rules.

mitnehmen: Net rental income is ordinary income reported on Schedule E and taxed at your marginal rate; there is no special rate and no holding period after which a gain becomes tax-free.

Depreciation over 27.5 years applies only to the building share, so the split between land and building is the most consequential figure in your records; it reduces your basis whether or not you claim it.

Rental losses are passive: with active participation, up to $25,000 can offset other income below a MAGI of $100,000, the allowance is gone at $150,000, and unused losses are carried forward until the sale.
On a sale, depreciation comes back as unrecaptured section 1250 gain taxed at up to 25%, possibly plus 3.8% NIIT; a 1031 exchange defers the tax, and a step-up at death erases it.
Rent caps exist only in some states and cities, but where they apply, they limit the return regardless of what the market would bear.

begriffe.text: Taxation of the part of a gain that results from earlier depreciation when a property is sold. For buildings, it is unrecaptured section 1250 gain, taxed at ordinary rates but at most 25%; for 5- and 15-year property, it is ordinary income under section 1245.

Trade or business in which you do not materially participate, and every rental activity unless you qualify as a real estate professional (26 U.S.C. § 469). Losses only offset passive income; the rest is suspended until a later year or a taxable sale. Owners who actively participate get a special allowance of up to $25,000.

Exchange of real property held for investment or business use for other like-kind real property without recognizing the gain (26 U.S.C. § 1031). It requires a qualified intermediary, identification within 45 days and completion within 180 days; the basis carries over.
Cost of a property plus capitalized closing costs and improvements, minus the depreciation allowed or allowable. The gain on a sale is the amount realized minus the adjusted basis.

Engineering-based study that splits the cost of a building into building components with 27.5 or 39 years and shorter-lived property such as 5-year appliances and 15-year land improvements. It brings depreciation forward; the accelerated part is taxed as ordinary income on a sale.
